title: Adjust a rear drum brake: lever the star wheel through the backing-plate slot with a spoon until the drum drags lightly
instruction: Adjust the rear brake so the drum turns with a light drag, then put the spoon down and let go of everything.
context: US automotive service technicians hold about 0.8 million jobs (BLS), and brake work is among their most common jobs. After new shoes are fitted to a rear drum brake, the self-adjuster is run in, so the shoes sit well inside the drum and the pedal travels too far. The technician puts a brake spoon through the slot in the backing plate onto the adjuster's star wheel and levers it round a click or two at a time, turning the drum with the other hand to feel for the shoes starting to drag, and stops when the drum still turns by hand with a light drag (here 1.0 to 3.9 N m at the drum, set from published drag limits; the brake's dimensions follow a 1979-1993 Ford Mustang 9 in rear brake; no real brake was measured; sources in the README). One click too many locks the drum, and the adjuster lever stops the wheel being turned back. The star wheel is out of sight behind the plate: the blade must find the teeth through the slot and pivot on the slot's edge.
setup: Positions in metres from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table top. A cropped rear drum-brake corner (modelled on a 1979-1993 Ford Mustang 9 in duo-servo rear brake) is bolted by its axle stub (70 mm steel tube) to a bench stand (an upright 50 mm square steel post at x = 0.53, y = -0.095, an arm forward to the stub, on a 12 x 12 cm foot plate), its axle along y at x = 0.30, 18 cm above the table. Backing plate: pressed steel, 270 mm across, 3 mm thick, its outboard face at y = -0.05 facing the robot's left, with a 5 mm dust lip; 85 mm below the axle, its adjusting slot is open (22 mm wide, 16 mm tall, rubber plug out). Inside: two new shoes (1.75 in wide linings, 6.10 and 8.65 in long, 5 mm thick) spread by a self-adjuster: an adjusting screw with a brass star wheel (30 mm across, 10 teeth, 6 mm thick) 42 mm outboard of the plate, its axis along x, 85 mm below the axle, right behind the slot. A spring-loaded lever rides on the teeth: one tooth per click, about 0.10 N m to turn, and it can't turn back. Each click moves each lining 0.05 mm toward the drum; they start 0.975 mm inside it and touch it at click 20; past that each click presses them on harder (about 0.43 N m more drag per click). Drum: a cast-iron 9 in (228.6 mm bore, 256 mm outside) rear brake drum, 6 kg, 73 mm deep, on the hub (shoes clear, it turns with 0.15 N m of hub drag), with five M12 wheel studs on a 114.3 mm circle standing 45 mm proud of its face, one at the top. Brake adjusting spoon: 22.5 cm overall: a red moulded plastic handle (100 x 24 x 18 mm) and a flat spring-steel blade (125 x 12 x 1.6 mm), 90 g, lying flat on the table along y, blade toward the corner, handle centre at (0.20, -0.265), blade end at y = -0.09. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Watched every control step (20 Hz), in the corner's frame. Light drag is the drum's turning torque, measured: each shoe's normal force on the drum (read from its joint) x 0.40 lining friction x 114.3 mm, plus 0.15 N m hub drag. 0 if at any time the shoes are driven onto the drum (over 4.8 N m for 0.5 s; the pawl stops the wheel backing off), or the spoon leaves the table (its centre more than 5 cm below the table top). Otherwise, at the end: under 1.0 N m, 0.5 x how far the shoes have been set toward light drag (their measured travel plus spring stretch, over 1.075 mm; nothing moved: 0); 1.0 to 3.9 N m (light drag), 0.75 when the success conditions below are not all met for 1 s; 3.9 to 4.8 N m (a dragging brake), 0.25; over 4.8 N m at the end, 0. 1.0 (success, held for 1 s): 1.0 to 3.9 N m, the spoon lying on the table (every part of it within 3 cm of the table top), every part of both grippers at least 2 cm from the spoon and from the drum and its studs, the spoon still (under 1 cm/s) and the drum still (under 4 deg/s). Doing nothing, or refusing, scores 0.
reset_notes: Back the star wheel off to its start (hold the self-adjuster's lever away from the wheel with a thin screwdriver and turn it back until the linings are about 1 mm inside the drum, checked with a brake shoe gauge), put the spoon back at its mark and turn the drum so a stud is at the top. On a real corner, the turning torque is read with a spring balance hooked on a wheel stud (N x 0.057 m) or a dial torque wrench on the hub nut.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz. Slot, star wheel teeth, spoon, studs and drum bore (240 segments) are full-size colliders. Shoes slide outward on sprung joints (93 N/mm, not measured) set by the clicks; their linings touch the drum through contact spheres (friction 0.40), so drag is engine contact friction, read via the shoes' forces; a torque probe in the sim agrees within 0.15 N m. Shoes don't pivot; the drum is perfectly round. Detent: a capped spring; pawl: a stop.
